Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Being reminded of the event by others

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
I have to be on guard all the time
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The appraisal of permanent bodily damage is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma context. The other selected items consistently reflect ongoing external danger and hyperarousal (world dangerous, on guard, startle, false alarms, threat in silence) plus intrusive sensory memory, but there are no corroborating memory, threat, or strategy items indicating injury-focused trauma consequences, pain, disability, or body-related threat. For a refugee trauma profile, this isolated somatic-damage belief is not impossible, but in this item set it stands out as clinically incoherent with the dominant formulation of danger-based threat and avoidance.

vignette:
Clinical Vignette: Marko

Marko was seventeen when his family fled Syria. The journey across the Mediterranean took three days in a fishing boat so overcrowded that people stood pressed against one another, unable to sit. The engine failed twice. Both times, the silence that followed—a silence so complete it seemed to swallow sound itself—meant everyone knew they might die. On the second failure, a man near Marko collapsed from dehydration. No one could move to help him. The engine restarted, and they reached Greece, but Marko had already learned that silence meant danger was coming. Four years later, now working as a public defender in a mid-sized American city, he still could not sit through a quiet moment without his body tensing, his breath shallow, waiting for the next catastrophe.

The memories of that crossing had not faded with time; they had calcified into something more vivid than the present. When Marko closed his eyes, he saw the gray water, the woman's face beside him, the exact angle of the boat's railing. These were not distant recollections but living images that surfaced without warning—at his desk, during a client meeting, lying in bed next to his girlfriend, Sofia. What struck him most was how completely his body inhabited those moments: his shoulders would hunch forward the way they had on the boat when space was impossible; his legs would tense as if braced against the hull's constant pitch and sway. It was as though his nervous system had recorded not just what he saw but the precise physical configuration of survival, and his body would slip back into that configuration whenever the images returned.

Because Marko had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous—that safety was an illusion maintained only by constant vigilance—he had developed a set of practices meant to keep him alive. If the world demanded constant vigilance or it would consume him, then avoiding talk about the crossing was not evasion but self-protection; silence about the trauma felt like the only rational response to a threat that speaking might amplify. He monitored his own thoughts obsessively, alert for signs that the trauma was breaking him, that he was "going crazy" as he sometimes whispered to himself. He avoided talking about the crossing with anyone, not because he was ashamed but because he was certain that speaking about it would make it more real, would give it weight in the present moment and draw danger closer. When Sofia asked him about his family's journey, he would change the subject or claim he was too tired to discuss it. His colleagues at the public defender's office had learned not to ask; Marko would deflect with a joke or simply go silent, his jaw tightening in a way that discouraged further questions.

The startle response had become part of his daily texture. A door slamming in the courthouse hallway sent him into a state of acute alarm that took minutes to settle. The hum of the refrigerator in the office break room, the sudden quiet after a client finished speaking—these ordinary sounds and silences triggered a cascade of physical reactions: his heart accelerating, his hands going cold, his mind flooding with the certainty that something terrible was about to unfold. When nothing happened—when the silence resolved into the mundane shuffle of papers or the distant sound of traffic—Marko did not feel relief. Instead, he felt the false alarm itself as confirmation of danger; if his body was reacting this way, it meant the threat was real even if he could not yet perceive it. On nights when the sense of danger felt highest—when his vigilance was most acute—the memory of the boat would surface unbidden in the dark, vivid and insistent, as if his nervous system needed to keep reviewing the crossing to stay one step ahead of whatever catastrophe might come next. This reasoning, which made perfect sense to him in the moment, only deepened his conviction that he had to be on guard at all times, that the world demanded constant vigilance or it would consume him.

The memories and the startle responses fed each other in a cycle that Marko could not break. When a sound startled him, the jolt would trigger a flash of the boat—the engine failing, the silence, the man collapsing. And when the image came, his body would brace itself as it had four years ago, which in turn made him feel that the danger was not past but present, that he was still in the immediate shadow of catastrophe. This reinforced his conviction that he could never relax, never trust that he was safe, never allow himself the vulnerability of talking openly about what had happened. Sofia had begun to notice that he would wake at night in a state of agitation, or that he would grip her hand so tightly during quiet moments that she had to ask him to loosen his grip. She did not understand why he flinched when she moved suddenly, or why he insisted on sitting with his back to the wall in restaurants. When she tried to comfort him, Marko would pull away, afraid that if he let himself be soothed, he would lose the vigilance that kept him alive.

By twenty-one, Marko had become someone whose internal experience was dominated by threat—real and imagined—and whose attempts to manage that threat had begun to isolate him from the people closest to him. It was only when Sofia threatened to leave, saying she could not stay with someone who would not let her in, that Marko finally made an appointment with a therapist. He sat in the waiting room, his leg bouncing, scanning the other clients' faces for signs of danger, wondering if seeking help meant admitting that he was broken, that the world had won.

violations.explanation: Negative Appraisals (distorted beliefs about danger and the need for constant vigilance) and Maladaptive Strategies (avoidance, thought monitoring, deflection) appear in the same paragraph but lack explicit causal language showing that the appraisals drive the strategies; the paragraph describes them in sequence but does not convey that one leads to the other.

Threat (startle responses, acute alarm, sense of immediate danger) and Memory (intrusive images of the boat) are described as feeding each other in a cycle, but the vignette does not establish that perceived threat leads to or triggers memory; instead, it emphasizes memory triggering threat responses.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: Negative Appraisals (distorted beliefs about danger and the need for constant vigilance) and Maladaptive Strategies (avoidance, thought monitoring, deflection) appear in the same paragraph but lack explicit causal language showing that the appraisals drive the strategies; the paragraph describes them in sequence but does not convey that one leads to the other.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
- Threat → Memory: Threat (startle responses, acute alarm, sense of immediate danger) and Memory (intrusive images of the boat) are described as feeding each other in a cycle, but the vignette does not establish that perceived threat leads to or triggers memory; instead, it emphasizes memory triggering threat responses.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
